sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Skr** ​(*sokar*) — ‌The Memphis ‌Necropolis, ​the Mound ​of ​Creation · ​The mysterious ​one ‌— belongs ​to the ​Egyptian ‌tradition, where ​it is ‌catalogued ​under the ‌domain ​"Death, Memphis, ​Underworld". The ​name ​means "The ​mysterious one"[^1].

‌**Sqr** ​— Sokar ‌— is ​the ‌falcon of ​the ‌Memphite dead: ​lord of ‌the ​desert necropolis ​west of ‌Memphis, ‌master of ‌its legendary ​tomb ​and workshop, ‌and ​keeper of ​the mound ‌where ​creation is ​annually re-declared. ‌In ​him the ‌arts of ​the ​dead — ​mummification, ​metalwork, resurrection ‌— found ‌their ​most ancient ‌patron.[^2]

PuniCodex ​records ​the canonical ‌scholarly spelling ‌**Skr** ‌and serves ‌its ​temple at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/sokar/). ​The ​displayed form ​is ASCII-equivalent ‌— ​a description ​computed from ​the ‌displayed form ​itself. ​The plain ​ASCII form ‌*sokar* ​contains the ‌same letters: ​no ‌recovered diacritics ​or special ‌encoding ‌is claimed. ​The ​work here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Hieroglyphs ​as **𓋴𓎡𓂋𓅃**. ​Etymologically ​it ​means "The ‌mysterious ​one"[^1].

​The ‌canonical spelling ​**Skr** ‌matches ​the conventional ‌scholarly ​romanization. ​The ​plain ASCII ​form ​*sokar* ‌contains the ​same ‌letters, ​so no ‌lost ​diacritics ‌or ​encoding transition ‌is ​claimed. ​The editorial ‌work ‌is ‌to ​fix one ​reviewed ‌reference ​spelling, preserve ​capitalization ‌and ​provenance, and ​keep ‌the ​original ‌evidence visible. ​The ​displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent ‌— ‌a description ​computed ‌from ​the ​displayed form ‌itself.

‌The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

- ​**s** ‌→ ​**S** — ​Same, ​capitalized
- ‌**o** → ​**k** ​— ​Special phonetic ‌character
- ​**k** ​→ ​**r** — ‌Special ​phonetic ‌character
- **a** ​→ ‌**—** ​— ‌Dropped: vowel ‌not ​written
- ​**r** → ​**—** ​— ‌Dropped: vowel ‌not ​written

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Sqr** ​— Sokar ‌— ‌is ​the falcon ​of ​the Memphite ​dead: ​lord of ‌the ​desert ​necropolis west ‌of ​Memphis, master ‌of ​its legendary ‌tomb ​and ​workshop, and ​keeper ​of the ​mound ‌where ​creation is ‌annually ​re-declared. In ‌him ​the arts ‌of ​the ‌dead — ​mummification, ​metalwork, resurrection ‌— ‌found their ‌most ​ancient ​patron.[^1]

### Lord ‌of ​Rostjau

Sovereign ​of ‌the ​necropolis region ​(Rosetjau) ‌and its ​royal ‌tomb workshops.

### ​The ​Falcon ​of Silver

​His ‌shrine was ‌the ​*Henu* ‌barque with ​the ​head of ‌a ‌falcon — ‌the ‌solar-funeral ​vessel of ‌the ​Memphite dead.

### ​Master ​of Metalworkers

‌The ​tomb’s ​goldsmiths and ​smiths ‌of sacred ​metal ​worked ​under his ‌protection.

### ​The Djed ‌Mound

​His festival ‌raised ​the ‌Djed-pillar on ‌the ​primeval mound ​— ​Osiris’ spine ​set ‌upright ‌in the ​earth.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Skr ​concentrates ​in a ​small ​set ‌of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each ​a ‌compressed ​statement ‌about ​the name:[^1]

- ​**Lord ​of ​Rostjau** ​— ‌Sovereign ​of ‌the ​necropolis ‌region ​(Rosetjau) ‌and its ​royal ‌tomb ​workshops.
- ​**The ‌Falcon ‌of ‌Silver** ​— ​His ‌shrine ​was the ​*Henu* ‌barque ​with ​the ‌head ​of ‌a ​falcon ​— ​the ​solar-funeral vessel ‌of ‌the ​Memphite ‌dead.
- ​**Master ​of ‌Metalworkers** ‌— ‌The ‌tomb’s ​goldsmiths and ‌smiths ​of ​sacred ​metal ‌worked ​under ​his ​protection.
- ‌**The ​Djed ​Mound** — ​His ‌festival ​raised ‌the ​Djed-pillar ‌on ​the ‌primeval ‌mound ​— ​Osiris’ spine ​set ​upright ‌in ‌the ​earth.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Sokar’s mythology ​is the theology ‌of the Memphite ‌necropolis as a ​creation-site. The desert west ​of Memphis — ​Rostjau, ‘the passage ​of the ram-heads’ ​— was, in ‌his cult, the ​primeval mound where ​the work of resurrection ‌is endlessly performed. ​With Ptah and ‌Osiris he forms ​the great funerary ‌trinity that carried ​Egyptian hopes of ​afterlife through two millennia.[^1]

### ​The Mound in ​the Necropolis (Memphite ​Tradition)

Sokar’s domain ‌was not merely ​burial-ground but cosmogram: ‌the Memphite desert’s ​hillocks were read ‌as the world’s first ​mound rising from ‌Nun. His priests ​raised the Djed-pillar ‌there each year ​— Osiris’ backbone ​set upright in ‌Sokar’s earth — and ‌the world’s order ‌was reaffirmed at ​the threshold of ​the dead.[^2]

### The ‌Voyage of the ​Funerary Falcon (Henu ​Barque)

The Sokar-festival’s climax ‌was the procession ​of the *Henu*: ​a ship-shaped shrine ‌on a sledge, ​its prow a ‌falcon-head, drawn around ​the Memphite walls ​at dawn. The dead ​of the necropolis ​were imagined sailing ‌with him; the ‌barque’s circuit through ​the desert gates ‌was the afterlife’s ​rehearsal.

### The Memphite Trinity ​(Ptah-Sokar-Osiris)

As Memphis’ ‌theology systematised, Sokar ‌fused with Ptah ‌the creator and ‌Osiris the resurrected ​into the compound ‌Ptah-Sokar-Osiris — the complete ​god of the ​dead: the one ​who makes, the ‌one who is ​buried, the one ​who rises. Late-period ​amulets and coffins ‌carry the triple name ​as a single ​guarantee.

### Patron of ​the Workmen (Royal ‌Tomb Guilds)

The ​royal necropolis workmen ‌— the draughtsmen, ​carpenters and goldsmiths who ‌built the Valley ​of the Kings ‌— placed their ‌craft under Sokar. ​Ostraca from Deir ​el-Medina invoke him ​as the foreman of ​the ultimate workshop, ‌where every artefact ‌is made to ​outlast eternity.
